concepts.description: Charts need words as much as marks: action titles state the finding, axis and chart titles remove decoding work, and direct annotations explain the points that matter so viewers do not have to invent the conclusion.
concepts.title: Action Titles and On-Chart Annotation

concepts.description: An unattractive dashboard puts viewers in a mindset that isn't conducive to use, but the fix is displaying the data itself attractively — not adding ornamentation, which is a distinct failure mode from ugliness.
concepts.title: Aesthetics Serve Communication, Not Decoration

concepts.description: Clean horizontal and vertical alignment (prefer upper-left justification for how-to-read chrome) and deliberate white space make a layout comfortable; center-aligned floating titles and stuffed margins make even good content feel sloppy.
concepts.title: Alignment and White Space

concepts.description: 3-D styling on business graphs rarely encodes real data and often actively hides it, since objects in front occlude — completely hide — objects behind them.
concepts.title: Avoid 3-D Effects and Occlusion

concepts.description: People judge circle/shape size by a linear dimension (like diameter), not true 2-D area, so encoding a quantitative value as shape area systematically distorts how much bigger one value looks compared to another.
concepts.title: Avoid Area Encoding for Quantitative Comparison

concepts.description: Beyond a non-zero bar baseline, an axis can mislead by being inverted, by cherry-picking the plotted time window, by spacing ticks unevenly, or by rescaling a second axis until an unrelated series appears to track the first.
concepts.title: Axis Manipulation Antipatterns

concepts.description: A bar's length is read as directly proportional to its value, so a bar graph's quantitative axis must start at zero or it creates a visually false ratio between values.
concepts.title: Bar Graph Zero-Baseline Rule

concepts.description: Shows the distribution of a set of values, not just a single summary statistic — necessary because sets with identical medians (or averages) can have very differently shaped distributions.
concepts.title: Box Plot

concepts.description: A dense, colorblind-safe replacement for circular gauges/meters: one bar encoding a measure, a tick mark encoding a comparison target, and background intensity bands encoding qualitative range.
concepts.title: Bullet Graph

concepts.description: Categorical axes are nominal, ordinal, or interval, and this classification directly determines whether the data should be shown as bars or as a line.
concepts.title: Categorical Scale Types and Bar vs. Line Choice

concepts.description: A measure can be perfectly accurate and still be the wrong choice — pick the derived value that directly answers the viewer's question instead of forcing them to compute it themselves.
concepts.title: Choosing the Right Measure

concepts.description: Prefer light backgrounds so attention stays on the data, but when a dark brand template forces a dark ground, invert emphasis logic — white becomes the standout, yellow becomes highly attention-grabbing, and grey still recedes.
concepts.title: Color Logic on Dark Backgrounds

concepts.description: A color or intensity is never perceived in isolation — the surrounding colors change how it looks, so color choices must be validated in the actual context they'll appear in, not swatch by swatch.
concepts.title: Color Perception Is Context-Dependent

concepts.description: Roughly 10% of men and 1% of women cannot reliably distinguish red from green, so meaning encoded purely via hue (especially a red/yellow/green traffic-light scheme) is invisible to a meaningful share of viewers.
concepts.title: Colorblind-Safe Color Encoding

concepts.description: Combine bars and a line in one chart when part of the data is best shown as individual values (bars) and part is best shown as overall shape (a line) — for example, monthly revenue and expenses as bars with profit trend as a line.
concepts.title: Combination Bar and Line Chart

concepts.description: A raw measure means little on its own; it becomes meaningful only against a comparative yardstick, and there is a standard taxonomy of which yardsticks are useful.
concepts.title: Contextualizing Metrics with Comparisons

concepts.description: A running-total chart can only ever go up (or stay flat), so it structurally cannot show that the underlying period-over-period rate is slowing or reversing — plot the per-period values when trend direction matters.
concepts.title: Cumulative Charts Obscure Recent Trend Reversals

concepts.description: Match a number's precision, units, and vocabulary to what the audience actually needs and understands — more precision or unfamiliar statistical terms only slow viewers down without adding value.
concepts.title: Customize Numeric Presentation to the Audience

concepts.description: A single-screen dashboard usually cannot hold everything needed to act on a finding, so design it for interaction — drill-down and slicing initiated by clicking the data itself.
concepts.title: Dashboard as Launch Pad

concepts.description: A dashboard is a visual display of the most important information needed to achieve one or more objectives, consolidated on a single screen so it can be monitored at a glance.
concepts.title: Dashboard Definition

concepts.description: Of the many ways to classify dashboards, the one that actually drives different visual-design choices is the role it serves — strategic, analytical, or operational.
concepts.title: Dashboard Role Taxonomy (Strategic, Analytical, Operational)

concepts.description: Maximize the proportion of a display's visual weight that actually represents data, by removing decoration and non-essential elements first and only then enhancing what's left for clarity.
concepts.title: Data-Ink Ratio (Reduce Non-Data Pixels, Enhance Data Pixels)

concepts.description: A practical subtraction checklist for default chart chrome — borders, gridlines, gratuitous markers, noisy axis labels, legends, and inconsistent colors — so data and labels carry the load without competing non-data pixels.
concepts.title: Declutter Chart Chrome

concepts.description: Separate dashboard sections using the least visually intrusive technique that works — white space first, subtle borders only when density leaves no room for white space.
concepts.title: Delineate Groups with the Least Visible Means

concepts.description: Label data directly on the chart wherever possible, instead of forcing the viewer's eye to bounce back and forth between the chart and a separate key.
concepts.title: Direct Labeling Over Legends

concepts.description: When actual and forecast share one time axis, mark uncertainty explicitly — solid versus dotted lines, lighter weight, region shading, and labels — rather than plotting one undifferentiated series that hides where fact ends and projection begins.
concepts.title: Distinguish Actual from Forecast

concepts.description: Use shapes for entities and lines (with arrows for direction) for their relationships to show process flow or org-chart-style structure — a distinct display need from quantitative charts.
concepts.title: Drawing Objects for Process Flow and Entity Relationships

concepts.description: Encoding a single quantitative value in two visual dimensions of the same object at once (e.g., both bar height and bar width) tempts viewers into inaccurate area comparisons and requires too much study to interpret.
concepts.title: Dual-Dimension Encoding Antipattern

concepts.description: When flagging a measure's good/bad status, use a small number of discrete states (roughly 4-5 at most) rather than a continuous or finely graded scale, or the evaluation itself becomes hard to perceive quickly.
concepts.title: Evaluative State Banding

concepts.description: Audiences often resist unfamiliar chart forms; win acceptance by articulating benefits, showing before/after, offering options for input, and recruiting vocal allies — while testing whether resistance is change-aversion or a real design flaw.
concepts.title: Gaining Acceptance for New Visual Designs

concepts.description: Viewers perceive ambiguous or incomplete shapes as closed and regular whenever reasonably possible, which means a chart doesn't need a full border to read as a defined region.
concepts.title: Gestalt Principle: Closure

concepts.description: Objects joined by a visible line are grouped together more strongly than proximity or similarity can achieve, making connection the right tool for showing relationships between entities.
concepts.title: Gestalt Principle: Connection

concepts.description: Objects that are aligned with each other, or that appear to continue one another, are perceived as a single whole — alignment alone can group table columns without needing grid lines.
concepts.title: Gestalt Principle: Continuity

concepts.description: A visual border or shared background fill makes viewers perceive the enclosed objects as one distinct group, and it works even when the border is very subtle.
concepts.title: Gestalt Principle: Enclosure

concepts.description: Objects located near each other are perceived as belonging to the same group — often the simplest and least visually intrusive way to link data.
concepts.title: Gestalt Principle: Proximity

concepts.description: Objects that share color, size, shape, or orientation are perceived as grouped together, even when they sit in different locations on the screen.
concepts.title: Gestalt Principle: Similarity

concepts.description: Borrowing a visualization form's implied structure or rigor for data that doesn't actually have that structure — like forcing a foot into a shoe it doesn't fit.
concepts.title: Glass-Slipper Visualization Antipattern

concepts.description: A color-density grid preserves the full spread across many parallel series (or time buckets) that a single aggregate line — mean, median, or a percentile — would collapse away.
concepts.title: Heat Map for Distribution Across Many Series or Over Time

concepts.description: Horizontal bar charts are the default for categorical comparisons with readable labels: category names run left-to-right in natural reading order and are seen before the data under a top-left-first scan.
concepts.title: Horizontal Bars for Categorical Labels

concepts.description: Line charts exist to reveal shape — trend, fluctuation, cycle, rate of change, or co-variation — not to support reading off individual values, so their quantitative scale need not start at zero.
concepts.title: Line Chart for Trend Shape

concepts.description: Every visual element costs mental effort; extraneous cognitive load is processing that consumes that budget without helping understanding, so clutter that makes a graphic look hard can cause the audience to opt out before the message is heard.
concepts.title: Minimize Extraneous Cognitive Load

concepts.description: Show recent history at fine granularity and older history at progressively coarser granularity, as adjoining chart sections, so a long time series still fits within the single-screen constraint.
concepts.title: Multi-Foci Time Display

concepts.description: Comparing raw counts across groups with different underlying exposure or population size can reverse the real pattern; divide by the right denominator before charting a comparison.
concepts.title: Normalize by Rate, Not Raw Count, Across Unequal Groups

concepts.description: Human perception is tuned to detect change, not the absence of expected change, so a monitoring display that only reacts when something moves will systematically fail to flag a value that should have changed and didn't.
concepts.title: Noticing Non-Events

concepts.description: When a categorical axis has no inherent order, sort its bars/slices by value rather than leaving them in an arbitrary or alphabetical order.
concepts.title: Order Categorical Values by Magnitude

concepts.description: Bars show individual values ranked largest to smallest; an overlaid line shows the running cumulative total, revealing how concentrated the contribution is across ranked categories.
concepts.title: Pareto Chart

concepts.description: Most preattentive attributes have a practical ceiling of about 5 reliably distinguishable levels, and hue tops out around 9 before memory for what each one means starts to fail.
concepts.title: Perceptual Distinctness Limits

concepts.description: Pie charts encode quantity as 2-D area and angle, which humans compare poorly, and are frequently misused for data that isn't even parts of a whole; a bar graph almost always communicates the same data better.
concepts.title: Pie Charts Are Rarely Appropriate

concepts.description: Plot reductions below a baseline and additions above it (or use empty outline for a gap) so direction itself carries meaning, then reinforce with matching label colors and deliberate stack order.
concepts.title: Positive-Negative Direction Encoding

concepts.description: Of the many visual attributes perceived preattentively, eleven are relevant to dashboards, and only some of them can express "greater than / less than" rather than merely "different from."
concepts.title: Preattentive Attributes for Dashboards

concepts.description: Certain simple visual attributes are recognized almost instantly and below conscious awareness, while everything else must be found through slow, sequential, conscious search.
concepts.title: Preattentive Processing

concepts.description: A fixed scale with a moving pointer preserves the whole range and the viewer's position within it; a moving scale behind a fixed window hides everything outside that window and destroys spatial/trend context.
concepts.title: Principle of the Moving Part

concepts.description: The same underlying chart can support different claims by restyling preattentive emphasis alone — and in live presentation, revealing or highlighting only the relevant slice at each step controls attention through the narrative.
concepts.title: Progressive Emphasis Across Slides

concepts.description: Whenever shaded area or length represents a numerical value, that visual quantity must be directly proportional to the value it represents — the general rule that explains why bar charts need a zero baseline and several other common chart distortions.
concepts.title: Proportional Ink Principle

concepts.description: Radar (spider) charts arrange a quantitative scale radially from center to perimeter, which obscures data a linear bar graph would show clearly, and are rarely appropriate for business data.
concepts.title: Radar Chart Pitfalls

concepts.description: Purpose-built to show whether, how strongly, and in what direction two paired quantitative variables correlate — something a time-series line graph of the same data cannot reveal clearly.
concepts.title: Scatter Plot for Correlation

concepts.description: Top-left and center are the highest-emphasis regions of a screen, so the most important, always-important data belongs there — and a logo or nav controls never should.
concepts.title: Screen Position as a Static Highlighting Tool

concepts.description: A secondary y-axis can plot two differently unit-ed series on one x-axis, but forces the reader to decode which series belongs to which scale and can imply a false relationship — prefer direct labels or vertically paired charts instead.
concepts.title: Secondary Y-Axis Alternatives

concepts.description: Unlike a dashboard tile that lives inside a persistent interactive interface, a standalone chart may be viewed, printed, or copied out of context, so its title, axis labels and units, legend, and data source must all be readable on the graphic itself.
concepts.title: A Standalone Graphic Must Be Self-Sufficient

concepts.description: Working memory holds only about 3-9 chunks of visual information at once, which is the underlying reason data that scrolls out of view is effectively lost to the viewer.
concepts.title: Short-Term Memory Chunk Limit

concepts.description: Encoding ranked or quantitative values as a rainbow of categorical hues makes every cell look different and nothing stand out; varying saturation of one hue preserves order, draws the eye to extremes, and stays colorblind-friendlier.
concepts.title: Single-Hue Saturation Over Rainbow Encoding

concepts.description: A dashboard must fit entirely within one eye span, with nothing requiring scrolling or navigation to a different screen to be seen alongside the rest.
concepts.title: Single-Screen Constraint

concepts.description: Relative size is read as relative importance, so equally important elements should be sized similarly and the truly focal element should be made conspicuously larger — never leave sizing to layout happenstance.
concepts.title: Size Signals Relative Importance

concepts.description: A slopegraph compares the same categories at two points in time (or two states) as paired values connected by lines, so relative increases and decreases read directly as slope without needing a second chart.
concepts.title: Slopegraph for Change Between Two Points

concepts.description: Repeat the same basic graph many times, each instance varying along one variable, to fit a three-variable comparison within eye span that wouldn't fit in a single graph.
concepts.title: Small Multiples

concepts.description: A spaghetti graph — many overlapping lines on one plot — is hard to track; fix it by emphasizing one series at a time, separating series into matched- scale small multiples, or combining separation with muted context lines.
concepts.title: Spaghetti Graph Strategies

concepts.description: A tiny, axis-less line graph giving quick historical context without a precise quantitative readout — ideal for dense dashboards where a full chart won't fit.
concepts.title: Sparklines

concepts.description: Placement should follow which data is most important, most urgent, or most needs to be compared to something else — not a default grouping by department or data source.
concepts.title: Arrange Dashboard Content by Importance and Use, Not by Org Chart

concepts.description: Stacked bars make the whole easy to compare across instances but make every segment above the bottom one hard to compare, since its baseline shifts with the segments beneath it.
concepts.title: Stacked Bar Chart Tradeoffs

concepts.description: Highlight always-important data through fixed screen position; highlight data that's only important right now through a preattentive attribute that changes with the data, and never over-highlight either way.
concepts.title: Static vs. Dynamic Highlighting

concepts.description: Dashboard icons only need to cover three meanings — alert, up/down, on/off — and each should use one simple, consistent shape with as few severity levels as possible.
concepts.title: Status Icon Design

concepts.description: Condense dashboard content by reducing large sets of numbers to summaries and by showing detail only when something falls outside normal range — without going so far that the viewer loses all ongoing awareness.
concepts.title: Summarization and Exception Reporting

concepts.description: Deliberately design for the comparisons a viewer actually needs to make — through proximity, shared color, and combined graphs — and avoid visual choices that accidentally imply a comparison that isn't meant.
concepts.title: Support Meaningful Comparisons, Discourage Meaningless Ones

concepts.description: Text excels at precise lookup of individual values; graphics excel at revealing shape and relationships — pick text alone when only one unqualified value matters, and graphics once shape or comparison matters.
concepts.title: Text vs. Graphics Tradeoff

concepts.description: A space-efficient display of large hierarchical or categorical data as nested rectangles, sized and colored to make outliers jump out — not designed for precise quantitative comparison or ranking.
concepts.title: Treemap

concepts.description: Test one well-designed prototype with real users and real data rather than presenting multiple design alternatives for them to choose between.
concepts.title: Usability-Test a Single Best-Effort Prototype

concepts.description: When bars represent counts grouped into ranges, unequal bin widths let bin width itself — not the underlying density of the data — drive apparent bar height, which can manufacture a visual pattern that isn't really there.
concepts.title: Variable Bin Width Distorts Bar and Histogram Comparisons

concepts.description: Form follows function in data display: decide what the audience must do with the data, then make that use obvious through highlighting at most about 10% of the visual, removing distractions, and a clear visual hierarchy.
concepts.title: Visual Affordances for Charts

concepts.description: Anything that means the same thing, or works the same way, should look the same everywhere on a dashboard — including which chart type is used for a given kind of data relationship.
concepts.title: Visual Consistency Principle

concepts.description: Used sparingly, preattentive attributes do more than make one element pop — variance within and across attributes creates an ordered path through a graphic so the audience reads the most important points first.
concepts.title: Visual Hierarchy with Preattentive Attributes

concepts.description: Data visualization serves two distinct purposes — finding patterns in data and presenting findings to others — and designs that work for one often fail for the other.
concepts.title: Visualization for Exploration vs. Communication

concepts.description: Fully saturated, "hot" color is a powerful attention-grabber precisely because it's rare — use it sparingly, or its power dilutes and viewers are kept in an unnecessarily stressed, pinpoint-attention state.
concepts.title: Reserve Vivid Color for What Genuinely Needs Attention

concepts.description: A waterfall chart unpacks a starting value into sequential positive and negative contributions that reach an ending value, making composition of change readable without forcing every segment onto a shared stacked baseline.
concepts.title: Waterfall Chart for Sequential Increases and Decreases

concepts.description: Plot data on a map only when its meaning genuinely depends on spatial or geographic relationships that a table or ranked bar graph could not reveal.
concepts.title: When Geography Belongs on a Dashboard
